title: Reuben and Gad Settle East of the Jordan
summary: The tribes of Reuben and Gad, rich in livestock, ask to settle in the grazing lands east of the Jordan instead of crossing into Canaan. Moses angrily compares them to the scouts at Kadesh who discouraged Israel. They promise to leave their families and flocks behind and fight alongside the other tribes until the land is won, and Moses agrees, warning that if they fail, their sin will find them out. Half of Manasseh also receives land in Gilead.
story: Israel has defeated Sihon and Og (chapter 21) and Midian (chapter 31), and now holds the high plateau east of the Jordan. For the first time in Numbers, some of the tribes want to stop short of the river. The request echoes the book's great failure: forty years earlier, a generation refused to enter the land at Kadesh, and Moses fears the same discouragement is spreading again. The chapter shows the new generation finding a better way, a negotiated agreement in which the eastern tribes commit themselves to their brothers. The agreement will be tested and honored in the book of Joshua (Joshua 1:12-18; 4:12-13; 22:1-9), where the eastern tribes cross armed, fight, and are finally sent home with Joshua's blessing. Their later altar by the Jordan (Joshua 22) shows how this division by the river would remain a source of tension.
historical:
The territory in question is the Transjordanian plateau, between the Arnon Valley in the south and the region of Gilead and Bashan in the north, well-watered upland suited to pasture. Many of the towns listed in verses 3 and 34-38 can be located with reasonable confidence. Dibon is modern Dhiban in Jordan, where in 1868 the Moabite Stone was found, an inscription of Mesha, king of Moab, from the ninth century BC (around 840 BC). Mesha boasts of taking Ataroth and Nebo from Israel and states that the men of Gad had lived in the land of Ataroth from of old. The inscription confirms that Israelites, and the tribe of Gad in particular, were settled in this region, though it also shows that control of the area passed back and forth between Israel and Moab.

The eastern tribes were the first to be carried into exile. The Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser III deported Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh around 733-732 BC (1 Chronicles 5:26), a decade before the fall of Samaria in 722 BC.
cultural:
Reuben and Gad are described as having very large herds and flocks, and the land east of the Jordan offered excellent grazing. Their request is practical, the kind of choice any herding people would make. Moses' objection is not that the land is bad but that their request would break the unity of the tribes and discourage the others from fighting. In the ancient world, a tribe that left its allies to fight alone was guilty of betrayal. The solution follows a common legal pattern: a conditional agreement, witnessed before the priest, Joshua, and the family heads (verse 28), with clear consequences whether the condition is kept or broken.

The renaming of cities in verse 38 reflects another custom. Several towns bore names honoring Baal or other gods, such as Baal-meon, and the note that their names were changed may indicate that the Israelites avoided pronouncing the names of foreign gods. The later clans of Manasseh named villages after their leaders (Havvoth-jair, the villages of Jair), marking ownership by naming.
literary: The chapter is built as a negotiation in several rounds. The tribes make their request (verses 1-5); Moses responds with a long rebuke that retells the Kadesh story (verses 6-15); the tribes make a counter-offer (verses 16-19); Moses states the terms and the warning (verses 20-24); the tribes accept (verses 25-27); and Moses passes the agreement on to Eleazar and Joshua (verses 28-32). Each round repeats and sharpens the key phrase, to cross over armed before the LORD, which appears again and again. The final section (verses 33-42) records the land given and the towns built. Moses' speech is a sermon in miniature on the book of Numbers, calling the sons a “brood of sinners” who have “risen up in place of your fathers”, a memorable reminder that one generation can repeat the sins of another.

outline.t: Reuben and Gad ask to stay east of the Jordan
Moses rebukes them with the memory of Kadesh
The tribes offer to fight before their brothers
Moses sets the terms; the tribes agree
The agreement is entrusted to Eleazar and Joshua
The land given and the towns built

doctrines.note: Moses warns, “your sin will find you out.” Sin is not only a private act but a power with consequences that catch up with the one who commits it, especially when it breaks faith with others.

The eastern tribes could not settle down while their brothers fought alone. The chapter shows that God's people are bound together in a common calling; one part cannot rest while others bear the struggle.

The agreement is made before the LORD, in the presence of priest and leaders, with blessings and consequences. It shows the covenant pattern of promise and obligation at work within Israel's own life.

words.note: Achuzzah, possession or holding. The Reubenites and Gadites ask for this land as a possession, and Moses grants it on conditions. The word describes property held by right, used of the land promised to Abraham as a permanent possession (Genesis 17:8) and of the burial ground he bought at Machpelah (Genesis 23:4). It stresses secure tenure, but here the tenure depends on keeping faith.

Matsa, to find. It usually describes finding something sought, and it appears in the request, if we have found favor in your sight. In verse 23 it takes an ominous turn: your sin will find you out. Sin is pictured as something that seeks and overtakes the sinner, a vivid way of saying that its consequences cannot finally be escaped.

Nua, to shake, stagger, or wander. In verse 13 God made Israel wander in the wilderness forty years. The word pictures unsteady movement, like the staggering of a drunk or the swaying of trees. Moses uses it to remind the eastern tribes of what unbelief had cost the previous generation.

christ: The chapter has no direct prediction of Christ, but its concern for the unity of God's people is carried forward in the New Testament. The eastern tribes are asked to fight for an inheritance they will not share across the river, and they do so until all are settled. Paul describes the church as a body in which, if one member suffers, all suffer together (1 Corinthians 12:26), and he calls believers to bear one another's burdens (Galatians 6:2). Moses' fear that one generation might repeat its fathers' unbelief is also taken up in Hebrews, which warns against an evil, unbelieving heart that turns away from the living God (Hebrews 3:12) and urges believers to encourage one another daily. The pattern of a people who must press on together to the promised rest points toward the church's calling in Christ.
questions: Moses feared that Reuben and Gad's request would discourage the rest of Israel. When have your choices made it easier or harder for others to keep faith?
The eastern tribes promised not to return home until every Israelite had received his inheritance. What would it look like to live with that kind of commitment to others?
“Your sin will find you out” is one of the Bible's best-known warnings. Why do you think Moses gave it here, in a negotiation about land and loyalty?
